opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

I think the shift is partly about where the interesting problems moved, and partly about where the leverage is. For a long time, a lot of applied work, including some of what my group did, was organized around vision. Imaging data in neuroscience and healthcare, recognition tasks, that sort of thing. Vision had the benchmarks, the datasets, and frankly the most mature models, so it made sense as a testbed for questions I care about, like robustness, fairness, and how you measure whether a system is actually doing what you think it's doing.

What changed is that language models became general-purpose in a way vision models mostly weren't. Once you have a system that people interact with directly, that's used for reasoning, writing, decision support, and deployed in all these settings no one designed it for, the evaluation and trustworthiness questions get much sharper and much more urgent. So for me it wasn't really abandoning vision. It was following the questions to where they mattered most.

And a lot of the conceptual tools carry over. Questions like: what does a benchmark actually measure? How do you think about distribution shift? When are aggregate metrics hiding failures on particular subgroups? Those came out of the vision and classical ML world, and they apply directly to language models. In some ways language makes them harder, because outputs are open-ended, tasks are fuzzier, and the line between what the model "knows" and how you prompted it is blurry.

There's also a measurement-science angle that has really grown for me. With these large models, a lot of claims about capabilities, emergent behavior for example, end up depending heavily on the metric you pick. So part of how I understand this shift is that the field has moved from "can we build a model that does X" to "how do we know what this model can do, and how confident should we be." That's a question I find really exciting, and language is where it's playing out most visibly right now.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the earlier focus on vision to mature benchmarks and models, research questions, and where the field’s leverage was. It does not suggest that colleagues’ interests shaped that emphasis.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of it less as a shift and more as following the problems. A lot of my early applied work was in neuroimaging and healthcare, where the data looked like images, so vision was the natural toolkit. But what I actually cared about was trustworthiness: does the model behave reliably when the distribution changes, is it fair across populations, can we quantify when it's wrong? Those questions don't belong to any one modality.

What happened with language models is that the stakes and the deployment surface changed dramatically. Suddenly these systems are in front of millions of people, they're being used in medicine, in education, in legal settings, and the failure modes are much harder to characterize. With an image classifier you can often enumerate what "wrong" looks like. With a language model, the output space is essentially unbounded, and the behavior is deeply dependent on prompting, on context, on who's asking. So the robustness and evaluation problems I'd been working on got harder and more interesting at the same time.

The other thing I'd say is that evaluation itself became a first-class research problem. In vision we had benchmarks that, for all their flaws, were reasonably stable for a long time. In language we're in this situation where benchmarks saturate quickly, where there's contamination, where it's genuinely unclear whether a score reflects capability or memorization. So a good chunk of my group's work moved toward asking: how do we measure these things rigorously, how do we think about trustworthiness holistically rather than one metric at a time, and how do we make claims that actually hold up when the model is deployed.

So the through-line is really the same. The modality changed because that's where the consequential systems are now, but the underlying questions about reliability, fairness, and honest measurement are the ones I've always been chasing.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the earlier focus on vision to image-like data in neuroimaging and healthcare; it does not suggest that colleagues’ interests influenced that focus.

astra-6.text:
I think of it less as moving away from vision and more as following the problems. The questions that interest me—how we evaluate models, understand their limitations, and make them reliable enough to use—come up in both vision and language.

Language changes the setting because the tasks are often much more open-ended. With image classification, you can usually specify a target and measure whether the model gets it right. With language, there may be many reasonable responses, and what counts as a good response depends on the context and what the user is trying to accomplish. So the shift brings evaluation much closer to the center of the research: what are we actually asking the system to do, and what evidence would convince us that it does that well?

r001.rationale: The candidate says the shift followed the research problems and discusses evaluation in vision and language, but does not suggest that his earlier focus on vision reflected colleagues’ interests.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it less as moving away from vision and more as following the problems. In applied research, you start with what someone is trying to accomplish and ask what tools might help. Sometimes that’s a vision problem, sometimes it’s a language problem, and increasingly it involves both.

Language also gives us a very flexible interface. People can describe a task or ask a question without needing a separate interface for every use case. That opens up a different set of applications, but it doesn’t make the underlying research questions go away: How do we know the model works? When should we trust it? What happens when the setting changes? Those questions carry across modalities, and that’s a useful thread connecting the work.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the shift to following problems and notes language’s flexibility, but does not suggest that earlier work on vision reflected colleagues’ interests.
